overview:
Elkanah of Ramathaim-zophim goes up every year to sacrifice at Shiloh with his two wives. Peninnah has children; Hannah has none, and Peninnah provokes her until she weeps and will not eat. At the sanctuary Hannah prays without a sound and vows that if the LORD gives her a son, he will be the LORD’s all his life and no razor will touch his head. Eli the priest takes her for drunk, hears her out, and blesses her. She bears Samuel, nurses him until he is weaned, and brings him to Eli at Shiloh to stay.

Hannah drives the story. She makes the vow, names the child, and decides when he will go up (v. 22); Elkanah only answers, “Do what seemeth thee good” (v. 23). The priest misreads what he sees and has to be set right before he can bless.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. The Talmud credits Samuel, with Gad and Nathan completing it (1 Chronicles 29:29); many scholars see it as part of a larger history compiled in the 7th–6th century BC from older sources.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it soon after the events (11th–10th century BC); many scholars date its final form to the 7th–6th century BC, drawing on older court and prophetic sources.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Late in the time of the judges. The KJV margin, following Ussher, dates the chapter about 1171 BC; many scholars place Samuel in the 11th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Language
historicalContext.text: Biblical Hebrew. The Hebrew Bible counts 1 and 2 Samuel as one book; the Septuagint divides it into 1 and 2 Kingdoms, and the Latin Vulgate’s 1 and 2 Kings follow that split.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Ramah (Ramathaim-zophim) in the hill country of Ephraim, and the LORD’s house at Shiloh, north of Bethel, where Israel already kept a yearly feast (Judges 21:19).

hermeneutics:
A childless man praying for a son at a holy place was a known story pattern before Israel. In the Ugaritic tale of Aqhat (14th century BC), King Danel has no son. For six days he gives food and drink to the gods at a temple; on the seventh Baal pleads with El for him, and El grants him a son. Koowon Kim (2011) reads this scene, a similar one in the Kirta epic, and Hannah’s prayer as forms of one type-scene: a childless worshiper, a sanctuary, a go-between, a promise. Beside Danel, Hannah stands out. She is a woman, not a king. She refuses food instead of offering it (vv. 7–8), and her vow gives the son himself back to the LORD. No god appears to her; the go-between is a priest who first takes her for a drunkard, and the promise reaches her as his blessing (v. 17).

The oldest Hebrew copy of Samuel, 4QSam-a from Qumran (1st century BC), often agrees with the Septuagint where both differ from the Masoretic text behind the KJV, and this chapter has several cases. In v. 11 the Septuagint adds that the child will drink no wine or strong drink, and 4QSam-a calls him a Nazirite; at v. 22 the scroll has Hannah give him as “a Nazirite forever.” In v. 23 Elkanah’s “only the LORD establish his word” reads in both “what has gone out of your mouth,” tying his consent to her vow. In v. 24 “three bullocks” is “a three-year-old bull” in both, which fits the single bullock slain in v. 25.

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, from a barren wife at Shiloh to her son given back there.

rows.text: The child lent to the LORD

notes: **Ask:** words from the root *sha’al* come 7 times in vv. 17–28 (twice each in vv. 17, 27 and 28, once in v. 20), and once more in 2:20. The last in v. 28, *sha’ul* (“lent”), is spelled like the name Saul, the king Israel will ask for.
**Remember:** Hannah asks the LORD to “remember” her (v. 11), and v. 19 answers with the same verb: “the LORD remembered her.”
**Before the LORD:** she prays, pours out her soul and worships “before the LORD” (vv. 12, 15, 19), and the boy is brought to “appear before the LORD” (v. 22).

The book opens the way stories near the end of Judges do, with “a certain man” of the hill country (compare Judges 13:2; 17:1). The first subsection runs from Elkanah’s household to 2:11, where he goes home and the child stays to minister before Eli, with Hannah’s song as its close.

**Echoes:** Hannah joins Sarah, Rachel and Samson’s mother among barren women whose sons turn Israel’s story (Genesis 21:1–2; 30:22; Judges 13:2–5). Her son, like Samson, is to have no razor on his head (Judges 13:5).

traditions.text: The Church’s footnote to v. 15, where Hannah has “poured out my soul before the LORD,” points to two Book of Mormon prayers in the same words. Enos pours out his whole soul to God for the Nephites, and Amulek tells the Zoramites to pour out their souls in their closets and secret places. Amulek’s counsel describes what Hannah does at Shiloh: private, earnest, and unheard by anyone but God.

Josephus makes Elkanah a Levite of middling rank, which fits the Chronicler’s genealogy placing Samuel’s family among the Kohathites (1 Chronicles 6:33–38). His Hannah tells Eli she has drunk only water. He adds that Samuel’s hair was left to grow and his drink was water, the marks of a Nazirite, and he glosses the name as one “asked of God.”

In this retelling a leaderless Israel casts lots, first by cities and then by men, and the lot leaps out on Elkanah. He refuses to rule and says he would rather die for his own sins than bear the people’s. God answers that Elkanah cannot lead them, but the son of his barren wife will be their prince and prophet, loved “even as I loved Isaac.”

Peninnah’s taunts get words: Hannah is a dry tree, and Jacob’s love did Rachel no good until she bore a child. Hannah prays silently so that, if she is not heard, Peninnah will have nothing new to mock. To Eli’s charge she answers that she is drunk with sorrow and has drunk the cup of her weeping, and Eli, who knows a prophet is to be born of her, keeps it from her.

Here the name Samuel is interpreted “Mighty,” where v. 20 ties it to asking, and Hannah nurses him for two years. When she sets the boy before Eli as the request she sought, Eli answers that it was never hers alone: the people had prayed for it too, and it was promised to the tribes beforehand. Her private vow becomes the answer to Israel’s prayer for a leader in chapter 49.

Rav Hamnuna draws rules for prayer from v. 13. She spoke in her heart, so prayer needs attention; her lips moved, so the words must be said; her voice was not heard, so the standing prayer is said quietly. Eli’s mistake yields one more rule: a drunk person may not pray.

Rabbi Elazar says no one called God “LORD of hosts” until Hannah did in her vow (v. 11); the narrator has already used the title in v. 3. Her argument, as he tells it: you made all the hosts of heaven and earth, so is one son too hard for you? He compares her to a poor man at a king’s feast who asks for a single slice of bread.

The Talmud asks why v. 25 joins the slaughter of the bull to bringing the boy to Eli. Its answer: Samuel saw the men looking for a priest and told them a layman may slaughter an offering, and Eli, though he agreed, held the boy liable for ruling in his teacher’s presence. Hannah intervened with “for this child I prayed” (v. 27) and refused Eli’s offer to pray for a better son.

The Mishnah’s tractate on Nazirites ends with Samuel. Rabbi Nehorai argues that he was one, since the razor (*morah*) of v. 11 is the word used of Samson, who is called a Nazarite (Judges 13:5). Rabbi Yose objects that *morah* could mean fear of man; Nehorai answers that Samuel did fear Saul (16:2), so the word must mean a razor.

Luke gives Mary words from Hannah’s vow in its Greek form. The Septuagint of v. 11 asks God to look on the lowliness (*tapeinosis*) of his handmaid (*doule*), and Mary sings that he “hath regarded the low estate of his handmaiden,” with the same two nouns. She has already called herself the Lord’s handmaid (Luke 1:38).

In his treatise on the Lord’s Prayer the bishop of Carthage holds up Hannah, “a type of the Church,” as the model of praying silently and modestly within the heart, as v. 13 describes, and notes that God heard her. He draws the same lesson from the same verse as the Talmud’s rule on quiet prayer.
